utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, the question is why you did not contact him. Why didn't you go up to him? Now you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you bear that in mind, not to name the specific names. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say it in any other way. How can I say it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall go into private session briefly, and we will redact from line 2 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the driver who drove you from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac, is it the same driver who drove you further?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that driver drove us from the time we were loaded up to Bratunac and Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And his name was Saban.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Saban was the one who was killed, who was in my truck, and who told us when we reached Bratunac, he was the driver -- he was the driver of a company. We were driven by a Serb, not by Saban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to school. They blindfolded you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did they put the blindfolds on your eyes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they tie your hands?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just a blindfold over my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was this blindfold made from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Some cloth from some shirts or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say that you took the blindfolds off from time to time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while people were getting up onto the truck. And later on, when the truck set out, we had to put them on again. Well, they asked, Where are you taking the people to? And they said, To Bijeljina, to the camp. And the people didn't ask anymore. And not to be abused anymore, we put our blindfolds back on ourselves when the truck set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You put the blindfold on yourselves. Why?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid because there was one man with a red beret. And whether he was sitting with the driver, I don't know, but he was there, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a total of four of them; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you said there were four of them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there were more. But when the dredger -- the man operating the dredger said he wasn't going to stay behind, three men stayed behind, and then they were told to go to the other field to kill the other men. But three of them were called by name, and the other one, the fourth one, by nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did they use to shoot with?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before you came there, were there corpses there already?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mass of corpses. Half a hall full had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Explain this to us. So you entered, and they put blindfolds over your eyes. You went across a ramp, into a TAM truck; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the hall, there's an auxiliary building, and they knocked down a wall there and pushed the truck up against this wall, like a ramp. Now, were they afraid that the civilians would see what they were doing and tell someone? I don't know. But, anyway, I saw on the spot that this wall had been broken down when I toured the area, and it was made of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your eyes were blindfolded, and then you got into the vehicle; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many steps can you take if you're blindfolded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very near. You just took two steps and you were in the vehicle, in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were the bodies lying, the corpses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were all -- scattered all over the field, because the people dropped down in the field. And when that location was full, they went to this other meadow which had been mown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the dredger doing there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Digging a hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I tell you that you were not there, what is your answer going to be?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, and I'm saying that with 100 per cent certainty. I went there. I can guarantee that to you, 100 per cent sure. And if you are guaranteeing something, then that is for yourself to say. I know that you can say anything, that what is true is not and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that young soldiers told you, and you said that -- let's have a look now. You said that -- Radislav Krstic, on the 11th and 12th of April, 2000, page 2683, 2683. And you said earlier on in the witness interview before the investigating judge in the Higher Court in Tuzla on the 29th of July, 1995, that these soldiers had said that they were Karadzic's young Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, someone addressed them who was closer to them, Soldier, that's what somebody said, and they said, No, we are not soldiers; we are Karadzic's bare-faced Chetniks. And they were very young. They must have been even younger than 18. I guess they were so poisoned that they wanted to hold their rifles high up at the door, and they would sometimes just fire at walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that Karadzic abolished the Chetniks and the Partisans?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we did not dare tell them that they were Chetniks. They used that word for themselves. And you know that some people are proud of the Chetnik name. You know, thank God, that Serbia equated Partisans and Chetniks. So that's it, one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that there is a pit and that corpses are on the meadow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that night they did not bury anyone. When I escaped, they were on the other side of the railroad. I didn't know. When I started running along the railroad, as I started running up, I thought it was a fly -over. There were cornfields there. In 1999, when I went to the site, there was still some corn there, there was some corn husks left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw that friend of yours, that colleague of yours. You said that in the interview, when you spoke to Mr. Kruzevski [phoen] in relation to the interview of the 26th of January, 1998, and the 4th of January, 1999. This is what you said: [In English] "And, furthermore, he stated that he did not see [indiscernible] who is mentioned in the following paragraph, and he only recognised his nasal voice." [Interpretation] So you just heard his voice. But did you say in that same testimony that you did not see any soldier.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was night-time. (redacted) -- well, there I go mentioning him now. Yes, I recognised his voice. That's 100 per cent sure. They were calling out to each other by names, because if you know a man for 15 years, as soon as he starts speaking, even if he's in a different room, and if you can hear him, you can recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you rise because of line 14, that will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thought that would be taken care of. It's just, for clarity, talking about the statement which was just put to the witness, 26th of January, 1998, I think just to be clear, the witness does say he saw soldiers who were young, less than 20 years of age, when he's talking about the gym at Orahovac, and later on he says that when he recognised the voice of the colleague, at that point he did not see soldiers that were behind him. So I just think it's important to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was clear already from his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise, then. I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, after that you encountered a Serb soldier, and you walked with him for a while. You knew who he was, and he didn't know who you were; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was my suspicion that it was a Serb soldier, but it wasn't. It was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that they were looking for you all night. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They did not look for me all night; perhaps for a moment or for a minute or two, they started looking for me. They tried to look for me, but they didn't look for me all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what you said.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, sir. The man who saw me there, I spent the night there when I fled. The next day, that same man saw me. But even on the next day, he did not introduce himself to me, and again I ran away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you said: Witness statement of the 13th and 14th of August, 1995, pages 8 and 9, and you stated the following: [In English] "He took his weapon and his bag, and I took some small piece of army equipment that I could not recognise. He started walking in front of me, and I followed him. I let him take some distance, and then I started to run away. After a short distance, I hide in some bushes. The Serb soldier, apparently joined by some others, was looking for me for some time, and they gave up. In the dawn, I decided to continue walking, and the Serb who was obviously looking for me the whole night saw me at the moment and shouted me to stop. I succeeded in running away, and he didn't shoot." [Interpretation] How is it that you know now that he's not a Serb, but you stated then, when your memory was fresh in 1995, that he had been a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm going to explain it to you now. This is the way it was: When I got there, I knew roughly where that place was. It was free. When I walked up to the first meadow that had been mown, I asked him, Is this such and such a guard? And he said, Yes. And he asked, Where are you going? I'm going from Srebrenica. Is there anybody else with you? No. And then he had some insignia on his clothing. He asked me whether I smoked, and at that time I did smoke. And he said, Take a cigarette. His cigarettes were down there. I mean, he didn't even want to offer me a cigarette from his very own hand, but I did take a cigarette. And he said that he was from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and I was afraid that he was a Serb soldier when I heard that. Otherwise, afterwards, perhaps a month or two later, a cousin of mine talked about something, and this man said, Well, you ask him whether I gave him a cigarette to light up or not. Well, it was only then that I realised he was a Bosniak, that he was not a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I'm not going to go any further. I really don't want to go into minute details, because all of these minute details constitute a major inconsistency, and I've been telling the witness that all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that for some reason you are a favourite witness, but you were not at the execution site, that you were not saved, and that nothing was the way you put it. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic, when you are saying that as if that is the truth, may you look at your own children dead. When you see them dead, the way mothers did when their children were killed, and this is going to be confirmed to you by a witness who found clothing by the grave -- could the Judge please move into closed session so that I tell you where they were found, those people there? Because, I mean, I would have to reveal the identity of the village. So let them just move into closed session so that I can tell you where the blindfolds were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it -- Mr. Nicholls, do you have some redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this handwritten note of Naser Oric that we got late last night, is it acceptable? Can it be admitted into evidence? We will have it translated. I think it has been translated. No, it hasn't yet. I mean, this handwritten note where he confirms that he is going to execute the Serbs from Sandici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with it when the witness will be excused. Sir, now your evidence has been concluded. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming all the way to The Hague to give it several times. We do appreciate very much. Now you are free to go. Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, let's wait for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to the document being admitted at this time. Obviously, it was not on the list. I know that happens sometimes. If the document came in last night, I don't know why I wasn't given a copy until the last break. I asked, just when it was handed, some information about what this is, where it was from, and was told nothing. So there's no providence, there's no translation. I don't know where it's from, and this witness didn't know anything about it. So I don't think it should be marked at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you like it to be marked for identification instead of being rejected?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this time, I think there's no foundation for it to come in at all. It should be rejected, Your Honour. It can be marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It could be marked simply for the record to show what document we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the purpose of just the translation, we'll mark it for identification and see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Before we hear the evidence of the next witness, I understand that Mr. Robinson has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be brief. This is a motion for a finding of a violation of the Prosecution's disclosure obligations, as well as the remedy of postponement of the cross-examination of this witness until Monday. So that's the motion that we're making and the remedy that we're seeking. I distributed for you a document that was disclosed to us last week, which is a memorandum from the witness, Ambassador Herbert Okun, concerning meetings he had in Sarajevo and Belgrade on the 20th of December, 1991. Herbert Okun is a witness who has been listed for a long time in this case. He's testified in 2003 in the Milosevic case, 2004 in the Krajisnik case. And as far as we know, this memorandum was never disclosed until last week. The Prosecution had been ordered to disclose all statements of its witnesses on the 20th of May, 2009, and of course it's under an obligation, under Rule 68, to make disclosure as soon as practicable. I point out that Ambassador Okun's testimony is primarily concerning the number of meetings he had with different people in Bosnia and Belgrade, including Dr. Karadzic, who he was meeting with on 36 separate occasions, and there has been no disclose of any memorandum by him of those meetings, other than this one. And in this memorandum, on page 5, it indicates that Dr. Karadzic told him that: "We will not fire the first shot, and assured me that I'm a doctor and a poet and not a soldier." And this was in December of 1991, before the fighting started in Bosnia. It also indicates that Mr. Okun had a meeting with President Izetbegovic on that same day, and the president told him that they were very surprised and taken aback by the European Community's requirement that they submit their application for independence by the following Monday, and they would have preferred to have waited until they could negotiate, but they were left with no choice from the European Community, and that Germany and the European Community had turned the process on its head, making the other steps more difficult. And this is consistent with Dr. Karadzic's position about how the war started, and we believe it's exculpatory both as to his intention -- he's alleged to be a member of the joint criminal enterprise by this period of time at which there was alleged intent to commit genocide, and his statements show quite the opposite. So we believe that there has been a disclosure violation, that this document was not provided to us. I understand that it's a very difficult process of disclosure for the Prosecution, given the number of documents, and we've said repeatedly that they've done a very good job of trying to meet their disclosure obligations. But when they don't meet it, we feel there ought to be a record of that and a remedy. In this case, Mr. Okun is supposed to testify in chief for approximately three hours, and we don't believe that the remedy of postponing the cross-examination would be a particularly difficult one for anyone. But Dr. Karadzic and his team have not had any opportunity at all to discuss this and the contents of this document, and to plan it and insert it into the cross-examination, and we feel we should be given an opportunity to do so. So based upon this, again, we don't allege any bad faith whatsoever on the part of the Prosecution. We would ask that there be a finding that there is a violation of disclosure obligation and, secondly, that we have this modest remedy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Albeit with that violation, if you could explain to me why you are not in the position, you as Defence as a whole, not in the position to start your cross-examination on the points which are not related to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we consider the cross-examination to be essentially a package in which we would like to have all of the material before we begin the cross-examination. It is possible to cross-examine on some topics and not others, but it's preferable for us to have the entire package of information before the cross-examination commences. And we believe that, in this instance, it's a very important meeting. It's one of the very first in the chronology. In fact it's the second meeting of all -- and we think that it would be -- to commence the cross-examination without this material would disrupt the preparation. Again, it's not a major issue, and there's also not a major remedy being requested, in terms of time, because the cross-examination wouldn't likely start until sometime near the end of tomorrow in any event. So we think that if there is violations of disclosure, it ought to be accompanied by some remedy, and that seems to be a very modest one that we're asking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who's going to deal with it? Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll deal with that, Your Honour. Thank you. There's no basis, either procedurally or practically, for any delay in moving forward, certainly not based on a general tenet that somehow, for any alleged violation, that there must be a remedy. The -- I mean, I'll focus on the practical aspect of this first, and then I'll deal with the procedural aspect. With respect to the meeting that Mr. Robinson has alluded to, it's two paragraphs. That can be, notwithstanding the suggestion that somehow it requires a rejigging of every aspect of the cross-examination, incorporated into a cross-examination very quickly, a cross-examination, in any event, that, as we know, will continue into next week. There's no practical basis whatsoever for continuing. On a more procedural note, this was originally brought to my attention as an alleged violation of Rule 66. It is not. I'm pleased to see that it has not been advanced as such. With respect to Rule 68, we disclose to the Defence on a wide basis as much as possible that might be considered by them to be Rule 68, but when it comes to an issue such as this, that is, we need a delay for something that purports to be Rule 68, it has to be examined with a practical eye in context. There's nothing new about the allegation that there was the allegation of premature recognition of Bosnia, and I would note that that appears in other portions of the journals of this witness. So it would already have been incorporated into the cross-examination to the extent it was considered relevant by the Defence. The same applies to the rest. This is not a matter, one way or another, even if it crossed the threshold of somehow being a technical violation, which it does not, for a continuation of the proceedings. That would be highly impractical and pointless. Having said that, let me also mention that I appreciate counsel's graciousness in noting the efforts that the Prosecution has made and continues to make with respect to disclosure, and I didn't want to disregard that. But as it happens, there is, in my strong view, no reason to continue this matter. We can take advantage of the time we have, and there is no reason why the information in these two paragraphs can't be quickly digested and assimilated into any proposed cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put directly, whether you can answer the question why this document had not been disclosed any earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can't say, in respect of having reviewed the document and making a firm decision on it. As I said, the original point of view by the Defence is that it should have come up in the course of looking for Rule 66, a position, I believe, that they have abandoned, and properly so, so it wouldn't have come up in that nature. If I can easily understand, given what I've said to the Court already -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Tieger, it was an oversight -- it was not omitted out of oversight, or it was on your purposeful decision not to disclose this document because it does not fall upon any category of the documents to be disclosed to the Defence? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was just brought to my attention this afternoon, Your Honour. I certainly didn't look -- personally look at this document and make a purposeful decision about it previously. It was disclosed pursuant to a Rule 66(B) request, to which the Prosecution responded with great alacrity, as Mr. Robinson has alluded. So it came up in response to a specific request under Rule 66(B) to which we responded very efficiently and very quickly. What happened before that, I'm not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I expected some more detailed explanation from you, that -- Ambassador Okun is going to give evidence about his meeting with the accused and several other leaders, and this is the very memorandum which deals with such meetings, so I was wondering why such document was omitted in disclosing if it is not out of oversight. But I did not hear anything in more specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in an effort to be as helpful to both the Chamber and, particularly, Defence as possible, the Court will recall that the Prosecution provided a list indicating those meetings that we would be -- that we intended to or anticipated we would be dealing with in the course of examination-in-chief. I'm not sure what Mr. Robinson was alluding to, but we did not indicate that this was one of those meetings. So it's not -- it's not that we said, We'll be dealing with this meeting, and then did not provide the document addressing that particular meeting. So perhaps there's a misunderstanding in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean that this falls upon the 66(B)(ii) material. I agree with you, it's not his statement -- prior statement of the witness. But whether it's 68 material or not, it's certainly relevant. I take your word. Just a second. The Court will have a conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter during the break and will give a ruling after the break. That said, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the break, I have to switch with Mr. Nicholls and also log on and log off. I was wondering if I could have just a few moments for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If we break now, we can go on until the end of today. So it's better to take a break now, if there's no opposition. So we'll take 25 minutes' break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had wondered if the Court would give me one moment to slightly expand on what I said. Part of the reason I wish to do so will be incorporated into my comments. It would be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, I wanted to do make it clear, if it wasn't clear before, that this document was disclosed on more than -- a week ago, to the best of my knowledge, I think on April 14th, so the Defence has had, what is it, nine days to determine that they needed an additional two days over the weekend to assimilate this document. Beyond that, it should have been brought to our attention before so we wouldn't have to address it on the fly. When it was finally brought to our attention, it was brought to our attention as a Rule 66 issue. The Rule 68 issue was raised only during the submissions. And in that regard, perhaps it could have been clearer in saying that the Prosecution has been very clear, I believe, in the course of its pre-trial brief, opening statement, and every opportunity it had to make clear that the prospect of a sovereign and independent Bosnia was anathema to the Bosnian Serb leadership and to Mr. Karadzic. And the circumstances giving rise to that situation, however, are -- not only do not constitute Rule 68, but are basically irrelevant. And if the Court -- the argument that the factors that gave rise to that situation constitute Rule 68 would lead us back to not only all the events immediately preceding it, but all the way back to World War II and, indeed, to the battle of Kosovo Polje. Now, those matters may occasionally be relevant in the course of examining witnesses and so on, but they are not Rule 68, nor are the very factors leading to the imminence or existence of a sovereign and independent Bosnia, which the accused opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour the point very much. With respect to the timing of the disclosure, the way the Prosecution has insisted on providing disclosure is to put a CD to Mr. Karadzic at the UNDU. And I didn't actually see this document until this morning because it's very difficult for us to get that CD from the UNDU out to someone on our team to be copied and distributed to the people on our team. So there's a problem in the timing of disclosure, mostly because of the way the Prosecution is choosing to make that disclosure. But, in any event, this is clearly a document that we should have had, one way or another, and we should have had it much earlier. And we believe that, again, we're not asking for a drastic remedy, but this is going to be a long trial, with a lot of issues, and we think that the Trial Chamber ought to make a point at this stage of encouraging compliance with the Prosecution's disclosure obligations and having some remedy when there's no compliance. And we think that if you do that as a matter of practice, that the disclosure will improve. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, we did not insist on disclosure via CD to Mr. Karadzic at the UNDU. We're happy to provide it to Mr. Robinson. Furthermore, Mr. Robinson is here with respect to procedural issues and perhaps how to formulate objections, not with respect to the substantive aspect of evidence and determining its impact on the proceedings and its role in the examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we heard enough. This is our conclusion: The Chamber has examined the document in question and is of the view that while it's clearly not an item that would be subject to the Prosecution's disclosure obligations under Rule 66(A), it may, indeed, be covered by Rule 68. As such, and in accordance with that Rule, it should have been disclosed to Mr. Karadzic as soon as practicable. The Chamber is concerned by the fact that a document of this nature was only disclosed to the accused so recently, and we would ask that you, Mr. Tieger, make inquiries within your team to find out why this was done, and that you make sure that we will not find ourselves in this position again. However, having said that, in view of the time, I think we are very unlikely to reach the stage of cross-examination of Ambassador Okun until late tomorrow or, indeed, possibly until Monday, in any event. We will assess the matter tomorrow and decide, at the end of his direct examination, whether to begin the cross-examination or postpone his evidence until Monday. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that, if I could just ask -- make one other request, and that is that we would ask that one of our interns, if possible, be allowed to be in the courtroom with us. We have an intern assigned to each witness to prepare -- summarise their prior testimony and statements, and also to prepare a summary of their testimony in court, and it would assist us with the references, as well as be a wonderful thing for the intern, to allow them to just sit here so that we can make a smoother presentation of giving references to testimony and prior statements, as well as benefit the interns, who are working for free and working very hard for our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind me how the order read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The order read that we would have two people here permanently, myself and Mr. Sladojevic, and that we needed permission before anyone else were to join our team in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider your request and give a ruling tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would it be important for the intern to be here now or when cross-examination starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it would be useful if they could be here now so they could hear any closed-session testimony. But it doesn't have to be this minute, with this witness. But in the future, we would like them to be here for both the direct and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could make yourself comfortable. Sir, Ambassador Okun, my understanding is that you have been here for some time, so I wanted to thank you, on behalf of the Chamber, for your patience in waiting here in The Hague until today to begin your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Okun, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me address the preliminary formalities initially. You have testified here at the Tribunal on a number of occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in particular, you testified in the case of the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik in June of 2004, that is, June 22nd through June 25th of 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, have you had the opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, and can you affirm that it accurately reflected the evidence you provided to the Court at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I have reviewed it, and it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is 65 ter 90005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, would you provide that same information to the Court if examined again on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 65 ter 90005 for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted. The number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And with the Court's permission, I would now read a summary of Ambassador Okun's evidence as admitted. From 1991 to 1997, Ambassador Okun served as the special advisor and deputy to the personal envoy of the United Nations Secretary-General, former Secretary of State, Cyrus Vance. Prior to his work in the former Yugoslavia, Ambassador Okun served for 37 years in the United States Foreign Service. His service included negotiating high-level treaties between the United States and the Soviet Union. Ambassador Okun and Secretary Vance were initially asked by the Secretary-General to address the conflict in Croatia in 1991, and their efforts led to the establishment of a peacekeeping operation on the 2nd of January, 1992, pursuant to what was commonly known as the Vance Plan. Because of fears that Croatia's conflict would be replicated in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in late 1991 and during 1992, Ambassador Okun and Cyrus Vance also met with leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the accused. Their role in Bosnia and Herzegovina intensified with the establishment of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, or ICFY, at the London Conference in August 1992. Secretary Vance and David Lord Owen were the ICFY chair persons, and Ambassador Okun was appointed deputy co-chairperson. From September 1992 until May 1993, intensive negotiations were conducted between the warring factions to advance the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, a plan eventually rejected by the Bosnian Serbs in May 1993. From December 1991 to May 1993, Ambassador Okun met with the Bosnian Serb leadership on approximately 50 to 60 occasions, including the accused at more than 40 meetings. During this period, the ambassador personally maintained a record of meetings in a series of note-books. He has provided these note-books to the Court. The notes therein are not a stenographic record, but do memorialise important aspects of the meetings and frequently quote participants verbatim. Ambassador Okun recalled that the accused frequently raised the following arguments in meetings: that the genocide of World War II had reduced Serb numbers and thereby justified their claim to land where Serbs were now a minority; that the Serbs were once again under threat from the Muslims; that the Muslims planned to rule all of Bosnia and Herzegovina via a high birth-rate; and that the peoples of the different ethnic communities could not live together because of too much hatred. In their first meeting in December 1991, before the conflict began, the accused told Ambassador Okun that if Bosnian Serb opstinas or municipalities were not tied to Yugoslavia, as the Bosnian Serbs wanted, war would result. After the conflict began, the accused told the negotiators that the Bosnian Serbs would stop fighting once the map was decided, and the allegation of territory therefore resolved. Ambassador Okun testified that the war aims of the Bosnian Serbs were: One, to have their own state; two, for the state to have territorial continuity and to be contiguous to Serbia; three, for the state to be as ethnically pure as reasonably possible; four, to have a special relationship between that state and Serbia; five, a divided Sarajevo; and, six, a veto power of any residual powers that may be held by a central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The ambassador and Secretary Vance received detailed information from ECMM, UNPROFOR, the ICRC and UNHCR about civilians detained in camps and about ethnic cleansing. This issue was raised repeatedly with the accused. In response, the accused would point to the genocide against Serbs of World War II or other crimes allegedly being committed by non-Serbs against Serbs. The Bosnian Serb leadership took negotiating positions that depended upon the demographic change recently caused by ethnic cleansing, described to the negotiators by Bosnian Serb leaders as, among other things, "accommodating ethnic realities." The Bosnian Serb claim to the Drina River Valley, for example, was based on ethnic cleansing. This position was also reflected in the accused's preference for solving controversial territorial areas through referendum which would favour the side which had committed the cleansing. The desire to divide Sarajevo was also a constant refrain from the Bosnian Serb leadership. The shelling of civilian areas of Sarajevo city was protested to the accused. Ambassador Okun understood the aims of the shelling to be: A, to terrorise; B, to use the shelling to physically divide the city in accordance with Bosnian Serb aims; and, C, to show the Bosnian Serb people that their army was powerful and, therefore, to animate them. The accused made it clear on a number of occasions that he had full control over both the Bosnian Serb Army and Serb irregulars. At one meeting in September 1992, he told negotiators that, "We can do anything. The 'army has unified command,' and, 'I have full power.'" That concludes the summary, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, by way of introduction to the Court, I would like to provide the Bench with some understanding of your background, albeit brief. I appreciate the fact that it's impossible to capture all the achievements of a lengthy career, but I think it's important to outline a few of the highlights. First of all, your career with the United States Foreign Service was 37 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, and it was extended after I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during that time, among other things, you served as United States ambassador to the German Democratic Republic from 1980 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You served as the deputy permanent representative and ambassador of the United States to the United Nations from 1985 to 1989?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during that time, during your career, you were also responsible for the negotiation of major treaties involving the then superpowers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in particular, you served as deputy chairman of the United States delegation at the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks with the Soviet Union, that is, the SALT II talks, which culminated in a signing by President Carter and President Brezhnev at a summit meeting in Vienna in June of 1979?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were also vice-chairman of the US delegation on the Treaty for Prevention of Incidents on or over the High Seas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We try to follow in other languages, and I then I could understand the difficulty, so could you put a pause between your answer and the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand. And since I've mentioned that myself repeatedly, I will certainly try to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that effort with regard to the Treaty for Prevention of Incidents, culminated in a summit meeting signing between President Nixon and President Brezhnev; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, in May 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were vice-chairman to the United States delegation on trilateral talks between the US, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union, working toward a comprehensive test ban treaty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before I leave your State Department service, I feel I would be remiss if I didn't mention one more highlight, and that is that while you were serving in the United States Embassy in Moscow in the early 1960s, is it correct that you were the person responsible, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, for translating letters from Chairman Khrushchev to President Kennedy?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, after leaving the State Department, you served from 1991 to 1997 as special advisor and deputy to the Special Envoy of the UN Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from 19 -- I'll return to 1991 through 1993 momentarily. But from 1993 to 1997, you worked on the dispute between -- or 1995, excuse me, worked on the dispute between Greece and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were special advisor to the International Commission on Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, I guess just to round it off, you also lectured and taught International Law and International Relations from 1992, first at Yale Law School for almost 10 years, and then at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me focus now on your efforts during 1991 and 1993. Can you tell the Court how you and Secretary Vance came to assume your responsibilities as special envoy and deputy to the special envoy -- to the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We were summoned and asked to take on that responsibility by the Secretary-General of the United Nations, then Javier Perez de Cuellar. It was in early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you explained to the Court in your Krajisnik testimony that you were tasked with fact-finding and then initiating a peacekeeping operation that could assist in reaching a cessation of hostilities in Croatia. I think you were quoted as -- you and Secretary Vance were charged with ending the fighting in Croatia. Is that correct, and is there anything more you were charged with that you need to bring to the attention of the Court?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: That is correct, except I should add that it was we who suggested the peacekeeping operation, and it was accepted by the United Nations Security Council after a cessation of hostilities had been achieved and had been accepted also by the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that cessation of hostilities began in January of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It began in November 1991, with the signing of an initial cessation of hostilities agreement subject to certain conditions, and those conditions were met. And an implementing agreement, which confirmed that and led to a complete cessation of hostilities, was signed in Sarajevo on January 2nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with the initial cessation, and then the implementing agreement, and then the complete cessation of hostilities in January, did your efforts in the region cease or continue?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: They continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was the focus of your efforts at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: There was several foci. The first was to -- excuse me, Your Honour. The first was to follow up on the implementing accord of January 2nd, in other words, the cessation of hostilities in Croatia, the arrival of the peacekeeping troops in Croatia, which was, I might say, the first time in history the United Nations peacekeeping troops had been active in Europe. That took several months. It did not happen immediately. It began in March, indeed, of 1992. At the same time, the worsening situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina drew our attention. And once the fighting began in March of 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were quite busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, just to set the context a bit, I believe you described in your earlier testimony that during this period, that is, late 1991 and the first half or so of 1992, as you and Secretary Vance were engaged in your efforts both in Croatia and Bosnia, the European Community was also actively engaged in efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution of the situation in the region; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The then European Community was, indeed, in charge of the overall political negotiations regarding the future of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that that effort took the particular form of what was called the Conference on Yugoslavia, which was conducted under the chairmanship of Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The conference began its work in July 1991, very shortly after the outbreak of armed hostilities between Croatia and then Yugoslavia, and lasted until August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what happened in August of 1992, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In August 1992, the British government, which then held the Presidency of the European Community, convened an international congress at the very end of August 1992 which had two objectives. The first was to recognise the failure of the Conference on Yugoslavia to resolve the problem. This had obviously not happened, as the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina was fierce. Second, it was to establish a new peace conference with both the EC and the UN together in charge of the effort. That was the conference which went forward and went into existence in the beginning of September 1992 and was called the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you indicated that the International Conference for the Former Yugoslavia was a conference with the EC and the UN working together. Who served on behalf of the UN and on behalf of the EC?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The co-chairmen were Lord Owen, David Lord Owen, former British foreign secretary for the European Community. And for the United Nations the co-chairman was Cyrus Vance, former American secretary of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your role in the International Conference for the Former Yugoslavia, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I was the deputy -- excuse me. I was the deputy co-chairman for the United Nations. Ambassador Peter Hall, distinguished British diplomat, was the deputy co-chair for the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can you provide the Court with a quick snap-shot of how you and Secretary Vance, Lord Owen, and Ambassador Hall went about the effort of trying to reach a peaceful settlement, and some idea of the intensity of that effort?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: The conference met in Geneva, Switzerland. It brought to Geneva all the parties to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina for round-the-clock negotiations. The parties met together. They met with us. We met bilaterally with the delegations. It was very intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with whom did you meet in that time? For example, did you meet with only the representatives of the warring factions or with other leaders in the area?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: We met with both members of the warring factions and other leaders, both from Yugoslavia and from other neighbouring countries. But primarily the meetings were with the disputants, the former Yugoslav parties, that is, the Bosnian parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in an effort to obtain as much information as might be useful in assessing the situation in your meetings with the various leaders, did you also meet with representatives of the international community, NGOs and so on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We met with the most senior representatives and those on the scene of the International Committee of the Red Cross. In addition, we had, as a subordinate group within our conference, Madam Ogata, the UN high commissioner for refugees. She was an active partner. And we also met with representatives of UNPROFOR, which was the name given to the UN peacekeeping operation in both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and others. We met also with nongovernmental organisations, and, for example, we met with Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the former Polish prime minister, who after leaving office in Warsaw had been appointed special rapporteur for human rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had access to all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I've already alluded, in the summary of the evidence you provided during the Krajisnik case, to the fact that you maintained journals or note-books or diaries during the course of these efforts. First of all, are those the documents we see before you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, they are these booklets in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court your purpose in taking those notes, your experience in doing so, and the nature of the entries.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was always my practice to take notes at important meetings over the years. It became essential in the former Yugoslavia, and was essential from the first moment there, because of the intensity of the efforts that Secretary Vance and I were making and the number of individual meetings we might have the same day. Many days, we began at 8.00 a.m. and ended after midnight, and we had, in that period, perhaps five or six meetings with five or six different delegations from two or three of the parties. And so in order to know who said what to whom at the end of the day, I took notes during the meetings. I did not dally because of the urgency. It was no secret. I had my note-books out on the desk, the way they are now, except that I was writing in them. I'm not a court stenographer, but having heard the arguments on all sides, very often the same arguments, it was easy, I should say, to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and get down on paper the essence of the meetings. And the journals, of course, proved very useful to the negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you explained, during your testimony in the Krajisnik case, that it's important for a negotiator to understand and -- well, first to make assessments and then to understand the people with whom they are dealing, their level of importance, their arguments on issues, their relationship to one another, their veracity, and that that is a skill that one perfects on the job. Is it also important to know the objectives of the persons with whom you're negotiating?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that's essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a result of your meetings -- your many, many meetings with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and with the accused in particular, were you able to identify the war aims of the Bosnian Serb leadership and were you able to identify Dr. Karadzic's war aims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you describe them to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, you've already mentioned them. If you want me to mention them, I can again. They were: To establish a separate state inside of Bosnia, juridically recognised, called Republika Srpska. Second, the Republika Srpska was to be a continuous territory, not be chopped up into pieces, and also to have geographic contiguity with Serbia. Third, the Republika Srpska was to be as homogeneous, ethnically - "pure" was the word that was often used by the Bosnian Serbs - as it could be. Fourth, the Republika Srpska was to have a "special relationship" with the Serbian republic, which everybody understood to include, if it were possible, even absorption into Serbia. Fifth, the Republika Srpska leaders were to have an absolute veto over any residual powers that remained with the central government in Sarajevo, because it was clearly understood that there was going to be some nominal government representing the entire country in Sarajevo. And, sixth and last, the goal was to divide Sarajevo between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs. The other parties also had war goals. Oh, and excuse me. You asked whether Dr. Karadzic subscribed to these objectives. I would say, yes, he did, as indeed the entire political body of the Bosnian Serb state, because they adopted most of these, particularly the geographic ones, on May 12th, 1992, at a meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. These objectives were not a secret. The Bosnian Serb side was quite open and honest with us about these goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, you mentioned that the other parties also had war goals. Perhaps this would be an opportune moment for you to identify those.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The other parties were not quite as extensive in their demands, but they had war goals. The Bosnian Muslim side wanted a unitary state, centralised powers, and Sarajevo with only residual administrative ordinances to be outside of the capital. They wanted a majoritarian rule, because they were already a plurality with 44 per cent of the Bosnian population in 1991, and they were looking forward to the day when they would be an absolute majority. The last point of their war aims was a disputed one, and that was whether and to what degree a Bosnian-Muslim-ruled Bosnia-Herzegovina would be an Islamic state. The reason it was an open question was that the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, the Bosnian Muslim party, was itself divided into a secular section and a more religiously-inclined section. With respect to the Bosnian Croats, they first wished to vote, as they did, to take Bosnia-Herzegovina out of the Yugoslav Federation, to declare independence. Second, they set up their own state, called the Community of Herceg-Bosna, a rough analogue to the Republika Srpska. And they also wanted territorial contiguity with their mother country, Croatia, and they looked forward to the day when, formally or informally, the Community of Herceg-Bosna would also have a special relationship, possibly even uniting with the Republic of Croatia. You see that certain -- in certain respects, the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats had parallel goals. Of course, in other respects, they were completely opposed to each other. But it indicates the complexity of the fighting on the ground, because you had overlapping goals. Sometimes the parties were in opposition, sometimes some of them made or tried to make private side deals. That was not at all uncommon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you spoke about territorial continuity, or the demand for territorial continuity and territorial contiguity with Serbia, by Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leaders. Did they ever provide you with -- ever draw out for you or provide you with some graphic representation of exactly what they were demanding?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Of course, we had in front of our eyes the military situation. To begin with, we knew where the armies were; where the line of confrontation was; where the Bosnian Serb forces, the VRS, were; and what they were interested in. Beyond that, we had maps drawn for us, by hand sometimes, by the leaders of the three parties; the Muslims, the Serbs, the Croats. And then there were official maps given to the negotiators at the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia as representing the desires -- the geographic desiderata of the three parties. So there was no difficulty in knowing which areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina the parties were primarily interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I ask you to turn to a meeting of September 10th, 1992. That would be 65 ter 06534, page 45, for the Registrar. And, Ambassador, I believe that would be the ICFY book number 1, the meeting that began at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we see depicted there a drawing of what appears to be a map. Can you explain that to the Court, please, and what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It is my -- a handwritten drawing of a map that Dr. Karadzic gave to us that showed the -- that had an overlay on the map that showed the Serb-controlled areas. The map was a map prepared by Mr. Henry Darwin, an English jurist who had worked with Lord Owen, and Ambassador Cutileiro in the spring and summer of 1992 on Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there was this map, and then over it Dr. Karadzic put an overlay showing the location of the Bosnian Serb forces. And I drew a rough version of that by myself in my journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of subsequent -- and let me -- before I go on, let me ask you: The area marked with lines, it is the hashed area, that was the area controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, according to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, and it was accurate. The Bosnian Serbs, at that time in September 1992, controlled approximately 70 per cent of the Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of subsequent meetings, did Dr. Karadzic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership make reference to this area and indicate whether it represented the -- represented portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina which it claimed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I ask you to turn next to a meeting of the 11th of October, 1992. Mr. Registrar, that would be 65 ter 06536, and it would be page 34. Ambassador, do you have that meeting in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to turn to the third page of that meeting that begins with lines: "Kara - 'Main problem, Tito's borders.'" And if you could indicate the nature of that discussion leading down to "draws map by hand."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: It was a constant contention of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Dr. Karadzic, that the Serbian people were ill treated by Tito in the drawing up of the republic borders after World War II. This was, in fact, not true, particularly not true with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose borders in 1991 were almost identical with those that had been established -- by Bismark at the Congress of Berlin in 1878. Indeed, the Bosnian border is one of the oldest in Europe, not just in the Balkans. Where it is true, that Tito, who, as we know, was half Croat, half Slovene, and no friend of the Serbs, where that is true is with Serbia itself, because Tito did, in fact, wish to reduce the power of Serbia within his state, and he did so primarily by removing -- I should say creating Macedonia out of the Serbian corpus. Until 1946, what we now call the Republic of Macedonia had been Southern Serbia. And Tito also granted autonomy to areas within Serbia, traditional areas, the Vojvodina in the north and Kosovo in the south. So it is accurate to say that Tito sought to reduce Serbian power within Yugoslavia, but it is not accurate to say that he did it in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He took other steps that the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats disliked heartily with respect to the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the border issue was not won.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you indicate in parentheses, toward the -- about the third entry of that page: "(Draws map by hand)." And, Your Honours, I made application, as the Court is aware, for the addition to the 65 ter list, of 65 ter 22791. If -- with the Court's leave, if permission to add that was granted, I would call that up at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give me the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. It is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And could that be depicted on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, this is a map you drew during the course of your Prlic testimony. Does this map -- is that your depiction of the map that was drawn by Dr. Karadzic on the 10th of -- excuse me, the 11th of October, 1992 meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it's consistent with what Dr. Karadzic drew. You can see basically it's a horseshoe shape around Central Bosnia, with a green area that's Muslim ethnicity at the extreme left or western end of Bosnia, called the Cazinska Krajina in Bosnia, and it was called the Bihac Pocket during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does this map then indicate the map that was drawn by Dr. Karadzic during the course of the discussion about the areas that were sought by the Bosnian Serbs, the areas that would be left to Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to describe those areas, on the outer part of the horseshoe, that is, if we follow the horseshoe area around, would the outer region be the areas given to the Bosnian -- demanded by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the right of the map, which is basically the Drina River border with Serbia, you can see that the claim was to the entire western bank of the Drina River. Up at the upper right-hand corner, in the Semberija, as it is called, there is the hook around the Posavina, that is to say, the very top of the map, which is the Sava River, dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia, and then to the western part of Bosnia, the large blue area, which was a largely Serb area. The difficult areas, from the Bosnian Serb point of view, were the areas along the Drina River. As you can see, there's a lot of green on this map, and green are the opstina or municipalities that had a Muslim majority or plurality. And, again, at the top of the map you'll see the pink ones, and those were the opstina where the Bosnian Croats were in the majority. And the reason those areas were vital to the Bosnian Serbs, and they made it known to us, was, again, they wanted the contiguity with Serbia, so that meant basically they wanted to eliminate the Drina River as a border. And, in the north, where the pink areas are at the top of the map, that blocked or, I should say, overlay the route from Belgrade through Bijeljina, Brcko, to Banja Luka; namely, the corridor from the capital of Serbia to the Bosnian Serb capital of Banja Luka. That was a constant theme mentioned by all the Bosnian Serb leaders and by General Mladic and others as being an essential goal and necessity. Central Bosnia was, as you see from the ethnic map, largely a mixture of Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim areas, and, therefore, it had lesser interest to the Bosnian Serbs, although there were parts of Central Bosnia that, indeed, were of interest; the Ozren Mountains, for example, and other areas. But the horseshoe was the essential shape of the future Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just so there's no -- sorry, I don't want to run over the translation. Ambassador, just so there's no misunderstanding about the map, we see both the horseshoe area that descends to the left side of the map down through the area marked "2." We also see an area that -- a line that goes up and has in cross-hatchings in it. Was that simply a mistake that was crossed out?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that was my error when I first drew this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, within the horseshoe, and on the map we see areas marked "10," "9," et cetera, there's also a diamond or a triangular shape. So just to make clear, with the exception of that diamond or triangular shape, to whom was Dr. Karadzic saying that territory should go?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Well, the expectation was that the central part, that is, the area within the horseshoe, would be controlled essentially by the Bosnian Croats, and that triangle was to be the area that the Bosnian Muslims controlled. Roughly, if you draw a line from Sarajevo to Tuzla, to Zenica, to Travnik, and down back to Sarajevo, that was the area that both the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs expected to be Muslim. And as you can see, it's not much of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I may, let me take you quickly to a couple of more references related to maps. First to an entry -- a meeting of the 2nd of December, 1992. That would be 65 ter 065371, at e-court page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Following our practice, shall we -- you tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we deal with the ambassador's note-book first, or you'd like to tender it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, I'd like to tender all of the associated exhibits. That would be one of them. We can take them -- we can recite the numbers for the Court, if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with them as we go along. I take it you do not object to the admission of the diaries of ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how about this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the numbers to those? I take it there are three diaries, or more than?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nine?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nine of them. So we'll -- we are not dealing with so many items. I take it there are some 18 or 19 items, in total, as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can hear, for the convenience, if there's any objection to any of the items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There's no objections, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no objection to any of the items on the 92 ter list for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit them all, and the number will be circulated by the Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just to avoid any confusion, I think there are 13 note-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one thing I want to clarify is that amongst the items, I included two excerpts of 34th session and 37th session from the Republika Srpska National Assembly. I take it you are tendering only those parts which were referred to during the ambassador's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I mean, I will say that I -- as I'll say again on other occasions, I think the entirety of those sessions will eventually be before the Court, are extremely useful. But in terms of the references during the course of that testimony, the Court is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Mr. Tieger, you also tendered the index of material, but it was tendered for the purpose of helping us as a kind of aide-memoire or as an index?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it will not be admitted as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's entirely appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for clarification, and thank you for your patience, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Might I interject a comment at this point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel said there were 13 note-books. In fact, there are 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. And I had asked for 65 ter 06537, page 29, to be called up. If that can be called up on screen, please. Sorry, that's the -- that's not the correct date. I don't know if I have the -- 06537 is the exhibit. Let's try 38. It would be page 29 of 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, that's a meeting of the 2nd of December, 1992. As you can see on the screen, at the page at the left there are -- there's a discussion by "CRV," who I take to be Secretary Vance, and then "DLO," who I take to be David Lord Owen. And if I could direct your attention to the fourth entry under "Lord Owen," which says: "Still in disagreement with Bosnian Serbs, who want one horseshoe area." Is that a reference to the same horseshoe areas that we saw before, drawn by first -- drawn by Dr. Karadzic in those two meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, if I could ask for 65 ter 45272 to be called up. And can the Registrar go to Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, during the course of your testimony in Krajisnik, you had an opportunity to view, with the Court, a video of Mr. Krajisnik, and describing a map and an overlay over that map. And is that the -- is that one section of that video that you see before you now?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does that depict essentially the same horseshoe area that we've seen before of the territory demanded by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I next call up 65 ter 11313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Robinson, when you said that you had no objection, it also -- you also referred to those additional exhibits to be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So all the items will be dealt with by a memo by the Court Officer later on. On that basis, let's proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to direct the Ambassador's attention to this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, what I want to ask you, when this map comes up, is to focus on the areas within Bosnia and Herzegovina claimed by the Bosnian Serbs, that is, the horseshoe area you described, and ask if those areas were solely or overwhelmingly populated by Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: In some areas, yes. In many areas, no. As you can see by looking at the map, this ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if you look to the right, to the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, namely, the Drina, you will see much green area which represents majority Muslim provinces. I believe, indeed, that there were seven Muslim -- excuse me, I said "provinces." I should have said "opstina, municipalities." There were seven majority Muslim municipalities on the Drina before the war, from Zvornik in the north to Foca in the south, and the -- there are very few Muslims left in those areas due to ethnic cleansing, and they form part of Republika Srpska today. The entire Drina is today part of Republika Srpska, including all of the formerly Muslim areas which are now Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the Muslims living in those areas, Ambassador, I want to ask you some questions about what Dr. Karadzic told you about them, what he told you about the Muslims. First of all, you explained, in the course of your testimony during the Krajisnik case, that Dr. Karadzic spoke to you about the Muslim birth-rate. Can you explain that to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He was concerned that the birth-rate of the Bosnian Muslims, which was, I gather, considerably higher than that of either the Bosnian Serbs or the Bosnian Croats, would, within a relatively short time, give the Muslim population an absolute majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And since it was known that the Bosnian Muslims wanted a unitary state, basically one man one vote, he was very concerned that this would disadvantage the Bosnian Serb community, disadvantage them seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, can I ask you to turn quickly to your book number 4 -- Vance Mission book number 4. It's a meeting of the 2nd of December, 1991. And that's 65 ter 06530, page 21. And, Ambassador, I believe you'll find the relevant entry at page 45 of your book.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And under the entry on the right page of the -- now depicted on the screen, which begins with -- which is marked above "Belgrade, 12/2/91," and then the second speaker is "RK," I take that to be Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fourth entry down?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN
